reference_title: Design, Analysis, and Testing of Laterally Loaded Deep Foundations that Support Transportation Facilities
chapter_title: Lateral Load Applications and Selection of Deep Foundation Type for Transportation Projects

sections.title: Lateral Load Applications for Transportation Projects
sections.summary: Lateral loads in transportation projects originate from vehicle braking, wind, wave/current action, vessel/vehicle impact, earth pressures, slope movements, and seismic events. Common applications include bridge abutments and piers, temporary and permanent retaining walls, noise barrier walls, slope or landslide stabilization, and sign/signal structures. Batter piles can resist lateral loads via the axial component but are discouraged in seismic areas due to lack of ductility.
sections.body: Lateral loads in transportation projects can originate from a variety of sources including vehicle acceleration and braking on bridge decks and approaches; wind effects on traffic, on bridge decks, and/or structures; wave and current action in rivers and streams on bridge piers; forces caused by debris and ice; thermal effects in integral abutments; vessel/vehicle impact on bridge piers and abutments; earth pressures acting behind abutment or retaining walls; slope movements; and seismic events. Examples of laterally loaded deep foundation applications include bridge abutments, bridge piers, temporary excavation support, permanent retaining walls, noise barrier walls, slope and landslide stabilization, and signs and traffic signals. Lateral loads can also include vessel impact on fender systems, scour undermining of piers, and liquefaction-induced lateral spreading. Scour does not apply load directly but removes lateral soil support, increasing unsupported pile length and generating additional moments. Seismic events add inertia forces and may reduce lateral resistance through liquefaction. Batter piles are installed at angles typically 1H:12V to 1H:3V and resist lateral loads primarily through the horizontal component of their axial force. Batter piles have been discouraged in seismic areas because they exhibit poor ductility in compression and tend to fail abruptly in shear; also, their higher stiffness can increase seismic load demand on the foundation.
key_points: Bridge abutments, piers, retaining walls, noise walls, and slope stabilization are primary lateral load applications
Scour does not apply load but removes lateral support, increasing unsupported pile length
Liquefaction reduces lateral soil resistance and may cause lateral spreading loads
Batter piles resist lateral loads through axial component; angle typically 1H:12V to 1H:3V
Batter piles discouraged in seismic areas — poor ductility in compression, higher stiffness amplifies seismic demand

sections.title: Types of Deep Foundations Addressed in This Manual
sections.summary: GEC-9 addresses driven piles, drilled shafts, micropiles, and continuous flight auger (CFA) piles. Most lateral load applications require foundations with adequate bending moment and shear capacity. Foundation types excluded from consideration include vibro-compacted concrete columns, unreinforced auger-cast piles, helical piles, and timber piles.
sections.body: Lateral load applications typically involve the application of significant lateral forces and/or moments on a deep foundation, resulting in significant internal bending moments and shear forces. Adequate design for such loads requires deep foundations with adequate structural section and bending moment resistance. For this reason, most lateral load applications involve piles or drilled shafts. However, micropiles and CFA piles, especially with permanent steel casings (for micropiles) and internal reinforcing, can also be used to resist lateral loads when those loads are not significant. Micropiles can also be used in battered configurations for resistance of lateral loads as well as for slope stabilization. Deep foundation systems not addressed in this manual include those with limited tension or moment capacity, such as vibro-compacted concrete columns and unreinforced auger-cast piles; and those not typically used in transportation facility applications, such as helical piles and timber piles.
key_points: Addressed types: driven piles, drilled shafts, micropiles, CFA piles
Lateral load applications require adequate bending moment and shear resistance
Micropiles with steel casings can resist lateral loads in battered configurations
Excluded: vibro-compacted concrete columns, unreinforced auger-cast piles, helical piles, timber piles

sections.title: Selection of Deep Foundation Types for Resistance of Lateral Loads
sections.summary: Foundation type selection for lateral load resistance involves evaluating subsurface conditions, design loads, scour/liquefaction potential, structural properties, constructability, cost-effectiveness, and acceptable lateral displacement. Deep foundations are preferred when lateral loads are large, overturning is dominant, or slope stabilization is required. Key subsurface factors include hard/soft strata distribution, soft soils at shallow depth, depth to rock, and groundwater. Bending stiffness and section properties govern structural suitability.
sections.body: Selection of the optimum foundation type involves considering whether shallow foundations are better alternatives. Shallow foundations are typically more economical but deep foundations are preferred when a competent stratum is not present within an economical depth, when significant uplift or lateral loads are present, or when bearing support may be subject to scour or liquefaction. Deep foundations are generally more economical when overturning loads are dominant, such as for noise barrier walls and sign posts. The factors to be considered when selecting deep foundations to resist lateral loads include: subsurface conditions and geomaterial properties; design loads; potential for scour or liquefaction; structural properties of the foundation elements; constructability; cost-effectiveness; structural redundancy; and acceptable magnitude of lateral displacement. Subsurface conditions affecting selection include occurrence of hard/soft strata, presence of soft soils at shallow depth, depth to rock, and groundwater levels. Piles or shafts with large bending stiffness are better suited to resist horizontal loads because structural resistance is mobilized with smaller deformation. H-piles must be oriented to resist primary loading direction. Constructability considerations include site access, available space, availability of local contractors, obstructions, groundwater conditions, contaminated soils, and installation noise/vibration restrictions.
key_points: Evaluate subsurface conditions, design loads, scour/liquefaction potential, and constructability
Deep foundations are advantageous when overturning loads are dominant
Bending stiffness and section properties govern structural suitability; orient H-piles for primary load direction
Site accessibility, obstructions, and contaminated soils may control constructable foundation type
Availability of local experienced contractors may influence type selection, especially for drilled shafts or micropiles

sections.title: Exclusions
sections.summary: GEC-9 does not address shallow foundations, axial capacity design, settlement analysis, foundation construction details, or deep foundation types with limited bending resistance. The document focuses exclusively on lateral loading of driven piles, drilled shafts, micropiles, and CFA piles.
sections.body: This manual focuses on laterally loaded deep foundations. Other considerations regarding deep foundations, such as the selection of foundation type for axial loads, the design and testing of deep foundations for axial loads, foundation construction, or other foundation considerations are beyond the scope of this document. Although this document is applicable to multiple types of deep foundations, throughout the document these may be referred to generically as piles/shafts unless a distinction is necessary. In the remainder of the text, the term 'foundation' or 'foundation element' is understood to refer to a deep foundation. Similarly, the use of the word 'pile' is understood to refer to a deep foundation element, i.e., 'lateral pile analysis' refers to analysis of deep foundations under lateral loads.
key_points: Axial capacity design, settlement, and construction details are beyond scope
'Pile' and 'pile/shaft' are used generically for any deep foundation type throughout this manual
Refer to GEC-10 (drilled shafts), GEC-12 (driven piles), GEC-8 (CFA piles), Sabatini et al. 2005 (micropiles) for axial design
